I'm a german sociologist using your Network-Package and the SNA-Package of
Butts and have some problems, perhaps you can help me.

I installed the network-package and read a network (containing over 2000
vertexes)

 

network <- read.paj("C:/test.net")

 

I wanted to generate a blockdensity matrix for the network. I have a
partition data set in pajek for the actors and wanted to use this partition
to generate the blockdensity matrix. I tried to read the partition as
follows:

 

partition <- read.table("C:/part.net")

 

I tried to generate a blockmodel

 

blockmodel(testnet, partition, block.content="density")

 

And got the Error:

 

Fehler in dimnames(o$blocked.data) <- list(plabels[pord], plabels[pord]) : 

  'dimnames' angewendet auf Nicht-Array

 

 

What am I doing wrong?  How can a create a "membership vector" ?

 

Kind regards

 

Richard Heidler

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Question on Latentnet/LatentnetHRT
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm currently analyzing Add Health data using Latentnet/LatentnetHRT. I
especially like the fact that latentnet is able to provide the likeliest
number of clusters in a given sample and can express individual's membership
in clusters in probabilities. The problem is, I have been trying to use the
program as described in Krivitsky and Handcock (2007) in the Journal of
Statistical Software, but it seems latentnet program has been updated to
such an extent that the codes used as examples in the article are pretty
much no longer valid. After some tinkering I have figured out how to use
ergmm command and plot the cluster structure in two dimensions but I still
can't find the way to use BIC information to find out the likeliest number
of clusters in a given sample.
I suppose I could run separate ergmm commands with different constraints on
group numbers (i.e., ngroups=1, 2, 3, 4... so forth) and then compare their
BICs as in the figure 6 in Handcock, Raftery, and Tantrum (2007) in the J R
Statist Soc A --where the x-axis is the number of clusters and y-axis is
BIC-- but given the time it takes to process a sample with 71 vertices it is
practically impossible to use this for any bigger sample. So what I would
like know is as follows:

- a command/options in latentnet (or statnet?) library that compares model
fit with a range of possible number of clusters in one go. Ideally, a flag
in ergmm option that addresses it...
- is there a working paper, monograph, or updated help file that supersedes
Krivitsky and Handcock (2007), which is rather outdated, unless I'm missing
something?

Thanks for the help,

Hyun

-------------------------
Go Myong-Hyun
Doctoral Fellow
Pardee RAND Graduate School
Santa Monica, CA 90401

messages.subject: [statnet_help] AW: SNA Blockmodeling
messages.body_plain:
Richard:

It looks like the blockmodel() function in sna is choking on the  
partition object. When you use read.table, it reads in the information  
as a data.frame, whereas blockmodel() is expecting a vector. So:

 > partition <- read.table("blockpart.txt")
 > partition
   V1
1  1
2  3
3  2
4  3
5  1
6  3
7  2
8  2

So partition is a data.frame with one named column (V1). You can  
access that column as a vector in one of three ways:

 > partition[,1]
[1] 1 3 2 3 1 3 2 2
 > partition[[1]]
[1] 1 3 2 3 1 3 2 2
 > partition$V1
[1] 1 3 2 3 1 3 2 2

If you pass that vector instead of the entire data.frame to  
blockmodel, it should work fine:

 > blockmodel(network,partition[,1])

Network Blockmodel:

Block membership:

1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8
1 3 2 3 1 3 2 2

Reduced form blockmodel:

	 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8
         Block 1 Block 2 Block 3
Block 1       1       1       0
Block 2       0       0       0
Block 3       0       0       1

Incidentally, you don't need to call gplot; plot will work just fine,  
since R knows that it's a network.

-AHM

--

Hi Rodolfo.  I'm not too familiar with the simulate.sisnetwork  
function, but I wonder whether you could provide a sample object  
(perhaps Cong110.g2 itself, or another if it contains sensitive data)  
that produces this error so that we could duplicate it.  Though  
occasionally we can suggest possible causes of bugs based solely on  
the content of an error message, it is usually impossible for us to  
diagnose problems like this without being able to recreate them.   
Also, if we can solve the problem after seeing it happen before our  
eyes, then the bug fix will make it into a future version, which helps  
everyone!

Thanks!
Dave

messages.body_plain:
Hi Rodolfo.  I found what I think are a couple bugs in the  
simulate.sisnetwork function:  I believe that the line

     mat[1:nrow.nonnull, 1:ncol.nonnull] <- matrix(s$newmat,
         ncol=ncol.nonnull)[,order(order.col.sums)]

is incorrect and that it should be replaced by these lines:

     mat[1:nrow.nonnull, 1:ncol.nonnull] <- matrix(s$newmat,
         ncol=ncol.nonnull)
     mat <- mat[,order(order.col.sums)]

in two different places.  Also, the  line
   mat <- matrix(0, nrow=nrow, ncol=ncol)

should be moved just inside the for loop.  If you "source" the  
attached file (which contains these modifications), then your code  
should run.  You might also read the help file for simulate.sisnetwork  
just to make sure this is actually what you want -- i.e., a network  
whose marginals are exactly the same as the one you passed.

One further issue:  If you were expecting 10 different networks, your  
code won't produce that -- there is something I don't understand about  
the way the "simulate.network" function processes its "save.networks"  
argument that prevents using it to simulate multiple networks  
(possibly another bug?).  If you want 10 different networks then the  
following code should do it:

  tmp <- as.sociomatrix(Cong110.g2)
  tmp2 <- list(rows=rowSums(tmp), cols=colSums(tmp))
  class(tmp2) <- "sisnetwork"
  sim=simulate.sisnetwork(tmp2, n=10, save.networks=T)

Hope this helps.
Dave

Jo?o

generalization to the ERGM case...

Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ergm
messages.body_plain:
Hello Jo?o --

This is a very fundamental problem in network analysis:  are there size 
invariant parameters that can be estimated for network processes.  That 
is, parameters that govern the generative process of tie formation that 
are independent of the size (and composition) of the network.

The problem is easy to understand even with a simple Bernoulli random 
graph.  The single ergm parameter in that case measures the log-odds of a 
tie -- essentially, a scaled version of network density.  So the question 
is what happens to network density as the size of the network increases 
(or decreases)?  One possibility is that the mean degree remains fixed. 
So, for example, as the population increases, people do not have 
increasingly more friends, they probably max out at a certain point. 
That would be the fixed parameter of interest -- the parameter that is 
invariant to network size.

You can estimate a fixed parameter like this, but it clearly depends on 
what you think should remain fixed. If you were to posit a simple model 
like the mean degree remains constant as network size increases, you can 
fit this with something like an offset term to control for the expected 
decline in network density.

There is no one-size-fits-all here, though.  It will depend on the type of 
network and process that you are trying to represent.

We are working on these types of models now, for an application in network 
epidemiology.  The capabilities will be added to statnet when they're 
working.

best,
Martina

messages.body_plain:
David Hunter wrote:
> Hello Jo?o.  It is not generally possible to do this kind of comparison, 
> especially in a way that allow things like hypothesis tests (is the 
> transitivity effect significantly different?).  That said, there are 
> some methods that people do use from time to time to make such 
> comparisons in logistic regression models, and perhaps someday in the 
> not-too-distant future we'll have an easy generalization to the ERGM 
> case...

Just to elaborate on Dave's point, the problem here is that many 
parameters have practical implications which are difficult to interpret 
when the support (i.e., the set of possible graphs) is changed.  There 
is a technical sense in which one can ask whether the MLE for the 
triangle parameter of graph A is larger than that of graph B, and it 
does have a conditional log-odds interpretation...however, this is very 
unlikely to map in a simple way to your scientific intuition about a 
"stronger" effect.  Thus, the conservative answer is that parameter 
comparison is not well-understood at this time, and probably should be 
avoided.

That said, there are some cases in which parameters have clear 
size-independent interpretations, and comparison can be fairly 
intuitive.  For instance, if your model leads to dyadic independence, 
most reasonable effects (e.g., edge covariates) can be interpreted in a 
size-independent fashion.  (Of course, this assumes that the model is 
correct, or at least that you are interpreting the parameters in the 
correct marginal way.)

Ultimately, the real problem is that the kinds of social ``forces'' 
parameterized by standard models (especially in the general case) have 
effects which scale in a non-obvious way with graph size.  A triangle 
parameter of 0.1 says, in essence, that the conditional log-odds of an 
edge are increased by 0.1 for every triangle which would be added by 
that edge's appearance.  In a small graph, there are not many possible 
triangles, and the impact of this parameter on triangle formation is 
fairly small (in a practical sense).  In a large graph, however, there 
are many ways to attain a very large number of ``pre-triangles,'' and 
the same 0.1 ``triangulation force'' will lead the entire structure to 
collapse with large probability into a clique.  (This is the degeneracy 
problem -- see David Strauss's 1986 SIAM review paper for an early 
technical argument, or Mark Handcock's work for a more recent take.)  To 
use an alternate (but technically justifiable!) metaphor, the ``freezing 
point'' of a large graph (vis a vis triangle temperature) is much higher 
than the freezing point of a small graph, and thus the former will 
become degenerate at temperatures at which the latter would be in a 
``fluid'' state.  One could thus find a small graph with a large 
triangle parameter (i.e. at lower temperature) and a large graph with a 
small triangle parameter (at higher temperature), and simultaneously 
observe a much greater manifested tendency towards triangulation in the 
latter than the former.

This apparent contradiction could lead one to assert any of the 
following: (1) larger social structures really do have something which 
reduces the strength of ``social forces'' like the triangle effect, as 
compared to smaller structures; (2) one's real measure of ``strength'' 
should not be the natural parameter value, but the corresponding mean 
value parameter (or some such); or (3) the triangle model (and others of 
its ilk) are not modeling ``social forces'' in an appropriate way (at 
least for large graphs).  All of the above have been kicked around by 
workers in the field, and each is probably meritorious in particular 
empirical contexts.  This is a fundamentally _theoretical_ problem, and 
has to be resolved by close attention to the properties of the process 
you are trying to capture -- it's not some little artifact which can be 
automagically ``corrected'' or otherwise brushed under the rug.

And now you know why Dave simply told you, "don't do it."  :-)

As far as other means of graph comparison, I discuss some of the 
alternatives in my recent AJSP review paper.  There are actually two 
ERGM-like ways to compare graphs at present, but both require the graphs 
to be on the same vertex set.  (One of these is supported in the netperm 
package, if you'd like to try it out -- it also works with valued data.) 
  Kathleen Carley and I have also used distance-based methods to compare 
graphs on different vertex sets, but the kind of comparison this gives 
is an omnibus notion of similarity (i.e., it does not separate out 
different kinds of underlying structural biases) and it is purely data 
analytic in character.

That's a long answer to a short question; hope it helps,

-Carter

Thanks
Jo?o
